description: Welcome to The Ace of Pentacles! We’re building a high-impact, fun-loving team. If you love merging creative engineering with rigorous problem-solving—especially anyone excited by aerodynamics, F1-inspired telemetry, simulation modeling, or space tech—this is your crew! We want sharp minds who love building practical, innovative solutions while keeping the energy high and collaborative. Let’s engineer something stellar together! 🚀
summary: PIEZO is an interactive map and dashboard for Phoenix, Arizona. It places NISAR L2 GCOV radar backscatter (HHHH and HVHV) next to USGS and ADWR groundwater records, PRISM rainfall, GRACE/GRACE-FO regional water storage and source-backed datacenter records. It addresses “Dancing with the SARs” by turning multi-gigabyte radar products into browser-friendly map layers, and by asking a human-driver question about water-resource stress near datacenter infrastructure. It is important because it keeps observations, modeled context and reported claims separate, so people can explore without drawing unsupported conclusions. Today it is a single date baseline, because the NISAR scenes available to us come from one acquisition on 28 Oct 2026, and the processing scripts are reproducible so more dates can be added.
details:
What it does: PIEZO has seven workspaces: Overview, Explore Map, NISAR Radar, Groundwater, Water Context, Facilities, and Evidence & Methods. Users toggle layers, sample NISAR pixels, search 7,272 groundwater locations (507 USGS stations and 6,765 ADWR sites), view rainfall and water-storage series, and open facility evidence profiles with their source documents.

How it works: Python processors read NISAR L2 GCOV HDF5 (Frequency A, frame 71, HHHH and HVHV), validate coordinates, units and masks, and write derived Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, GeoJSON, JSON and CSV products with manifests. A FastAPI backend serves the catalog, evidence records, map layers and NISAR pixel sampling. A React, TypeScript and Vite frontend renders the map with MapLibre GL JS and the charts with Apache ECharts. Source files are never modified.

Benefits: Every layer keeps its source, date, units and spatial scale visible. Missing values are shown as evidence gaps and are never treated as zero. A glossary separates depth-to-water from water-level elevation, and withdrawal from consumption.

What we hope to achieve: A transparent starting point for investigating water stress. It does not claim causation, and it does not estimate data-centre water use.

Limitations: There is one NISAR date and no temporal change analysis yet, and radar backscatter does not measure groundwater. ADWR source codes are undecoded, and the facility register is small.

Tools: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic, h5py, NumPy, Rasterio, pyproj, Shapely, pandas, xarray, netCDF4, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, Cloudflare Pages, Render and Cloudflare R2.
